blocks.text: Jesus answers the lawyer’s attempt to limit the meaning of “neighbor” by making mercy concrete: the Samaritan acts for the wounded man when others do not. The story presents compassion as crossing a boundary rather than as an abstract definition, and it should not be used to make real Samaritans a mere foil for supposedly deficient Judaism.

Jesus’ statement that he saw Satan fall from heaven should not automatically be read as a direct reference to Isaiah’s “morning star, son of dawn.” In Isaiah, that poem is framed as a taunt against the king of Babylon; identifying its figure with Satan belongs to later Jewish and especially Christian reception rather than to Isaiah’s explicit addressee.

“The laborer is worthy of his hire” recognizes that those sent out to work may receive provision. A related, disputed discussion of “double honor” for elders understands honor as possibly including remuneration, while also cautioning that such support does not create clerical entitlement or place leaders beyond scrutiny.

Mary’s listening and Martha’s burdened hospitality create a scene about attention, anxiety, work, and discipleship. Jesus’ response need not demean domestic labor or confine women to a single role; the passage contrasts Martha’s troubled distraction with Mary’s chosen attention to Jesus’ teaching.
